chunks: "No, LiPos aren't forever. They wear out in two ways: from cycling, and just from sitting there, which we call calendar aging.
As they age, two things happen: the usable capacity falls, and the internal resistance rises.
A typical cell is considered at end of life when it hits about 80 percent of its original capacity, which might be roughly 300 to 1000 full cycles for LCO or NMC, and a few thousand for LiFePO4.
On the graphite anode a protective film called the SEI keeps growing slowly, and every bit that grows consumes lithium and electrolyte, so capacity falls and resistance rises.
Charging fast or in the cold can plate metallic lithium.
The cathode slowly degrades too, especially at high voltage, and the electrolyte decomposes and makes gas, which is why pouch cells swell.
What speeds it up: heat, being stored at high state of charge, high charge and discharge currents, deep cycles, and overcharging.

So to make a battery last, keep it cool, avoid sitting at 100 percent, don't charge it cold, limit the charge voltage a little if you can trade capacity for life, and use a fuel gauge to track health.
And when it swells, gets hot, or the capacity has fallen too far, you retire it."
